\section*{Question 6}
\begin{itemize}
\item[(a)] \(f^{\prime}(x)=-2 \sin (2 x)+\cos x e^{\sin x}\)
\[
f^{\prime}(\pi)=-2 \sin (2 \pi)+\cos \pi e^{\sin \pi}=-1
\]
\item[(b)] \(k^{\prime}(x)=h^{\prime}(f(x)) \cdot f^{\prime}(x)\)
\[
\begin{aligned}
k^{\prime}(\pi) & =h^{\prime}(f(\pi)) \cdot f^{\prime}(\pi)=h^{\prime}(2) \cdot(-1) \\
& =\left(-\frac{1}{3}\right)(-1)=\frac{1}{3}
\end{aligned}
\]
\item[(c)] \(m^{\prime}(x)=-2 g^{\prime}(-2 x) \cdot h(x)+g(-2 x) \cdot h^{\prime}(x)\)
\[
\begin{aligned}
m^{\prime}(2) & =-2 g^{\prime}(-4) \cdot h(2)+g(-4) \cdot h^{\prime}(2) \\
& =-2(-1)\left(-\frac{2}{3}\right)+5\left(-\frac{1}{3}\right)=-3
\end{aligned}
\]
\item[(d)] \(g\) is differentiable. \(\Rightarrow g\) is continuous on the interval \([-5,-3]\).
\[
\frac{g(-3)-g(-5)}{-3-(-5)}=\frac{2-10}{2}=-4
\]
Therefore, by the Mean Value Theorem, there is at least one value \(c\), \(-5<c<-3\), such that \(g^{\prime}(c)=-4\).
\end{itemize}
